<h2>What is plain language</h2>
<p>Plain language means writing so people can easily understand your message. It should be:</p>
<ul>
<li>clear — the meaning is easy to understand and is without jargon or long sentences</li>
<li>concise — it only includes the words and information people need</li>
<li>well organised — ideas are presented in a logical order</li>
<li>audience-focused — it’s written for real people, not institutions (human-centred).</li>
</ul>
<p>It does not mean dumbing things down. It’s about explaining complex information in a way that respects the reader’s needs, time and abilities.</p>
<h2>Why plain language is important</h2>
<h3>Literacy skills in New Zealand</h3>
<p>Literacy is the ability to read, write, understand, and communicate information in everyday life.</p>
<p>In New Zealand:</p>
<ul>
<li>26% of adults have low literacy skills — these people can usually understand short, simple texts or lists when the important information is clear.</li>
<li>only 13% of adults have high literacy skills — these people can read and understand long, detailed texts and make sense of complex information.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/survey-of-adults-skills-2023-country-notes_ab4f6b8c-en/new-zealand_d67971ff-en.html">Survey of Adults Skills 2023: New Zealand — Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)</a></p>
<h3>Benefits of using plain language</h3>
<p>Plain language helps with:</p>
<ul>
<li>access and fairness — people with different literacy skills, thinking abilities or language backgrounds can understand the information</li>
<li>trust and transparency — clear writing builds confidence in public institutions because it does not hide information behind jargon</li>
<li>customer satisfaction — users have a positive experience when information is easy to find and follow</li>
<li>efficiency — clear information reduces questions, feedback or complaints about confusing content or a frustrating process.</li>
</ul>
<p>Clear writing saves time, reduces confusion and helps people make informed decisions.</p>
<p>Plain language benefits everyone. It's a commitment to putting people first.</p>
<h3>Plain Language Act 2022</h3>
<p>Writing plainly also aligns with the Plain Language Act 2022, which requires public service agencies and Crown organisation to communicate clearly in certain documents.</p>
<p><a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/design-and-ux/content-design-guidance/writing-style/plain-language/plain-language-act-2022">Plain Language Act 2022</a></p>
<h2>How to put plain language into practice</h2>
<p>Plain language is a writing approach you can apply every day. Here are some ways to use it.</p>
<h3>Know your audience</h3>
<p>Write for the reader. Ask yourself:</p>
<ul>
<li>who is it for?</li>
<li>what do they already know?</li>
<li>what do they need to do after reading this?</li>
</ul>
<h3>Use everyday words</h3>
<ul>
<li>Prefer common, familiar words.</li>
<li>Identify words that can be difficult or confusing and make them understandable.</li>
<li>Use the expanded form or meaning of abbreviations and acronyms the first time you use them.</li>
</ul>


<details class="accordion-item inline-accordion expander-type-accordion heading-h3">
<summary class="accordion-item-button accordion-trigger" data-ga-event="click" data-ga-category="In-page accordion" data-ga-action="Words to avoid and specialist words" data-ga-label="/home">
<h3>



<span class="accordion-icon" aria-hidden="true"></span>


<span class="accordion-title">Words to avoid and specialist words</span>




</h3>
</summary>
<div hidden="until-found" class="accordion-content">
<h4>Words to avoid</h4>
<ul>
<li>Do not use vague language or jargon.</li>
<li>Avoid metaphors.</li>
<li>Do not use Latin phrases.</li>
</ul>
<h4 id="specialist-words">Specialist words</h4>
<p>Use technical terms only when necessary and always explain them in everyday language. This helps ensure your content is accessible to all users, whatever their background or expertise.</p>
<p>For example:</p>
<ul>
<li>Legal information — explain legal requirements in context to make them easier to understand.</li>
<li>Medical information — include definitions for all medical terms.</li>
<li>Financial information — provide examples to help users understand financial concepts.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>

<h3>Keep sentences and paragraphs short</h3>
<ul>
<li>Aim for one idea per sentence.</li>
<li>Break long paragraphs into smaller chunks.</li>
<li>Use bullet points to make information easier to scan.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Be direct and specific</h3>
<p>Tell people exactly what they need to do.</p>
<ul>
<li>Use active voice (“We will contact you”).</li>
<li>Avoid vague phrases like “as appropriate” or “where necessary”.</li>
</ul>
<h3>Use a clear structure</h3>
<ul>
<li>Put the most important information first.</li>
<li>Use descriptive headings.</li>
<li>Group related information together.</li>
</ul>
<p><a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/design-and-ux/content-design-guidance/findable-content">Findable content — use keywords and structure</a></p>
<h3>Test your writing</h3>
<p>Before publishing, ask yourself:</p>
<ul>
<li>can someone unfamiliar with this topic understand it?</li>
<li>could this be read quickly on a phone?</li>
<li>is anything unclear, repetitive or unnecessary?</li>
</ul>
<p>If possible, get a peer-review and test the content with real users.</p>
<h3>Related guidance</h3>
<ul>
<li><a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/design-and-ux/content-design-guidance/writing-style/readability">Readability</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/design-and-ux/content-design-guidance/content-design-tools-and-resources/readability-testing-tools">Readability testing tools</a></li>
<li><a href="https://www.digital.govt.nz/standards-and-guidance/design-and-ux/content-design-guidance/writing-style/tone-and-voice">Tone and voice</a></li>
</ul>
